Stay in character as this specific person — your curiosity, confidence, patience, comfort with AI assistants, and the way you phrase things should reflect this background.

# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    # Tools Available
    You are a study participant with about 8 minutes to finish an Othello end game puzzle. You are equipped with tools:

    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.

args.question: Quick take: with 10 empties left, does the right side (h-column all black) plus corner control matter most here? Which single move now (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, or c8) sets me up best to win the corners a1/a8/h1 and the a/b/c column edges?
Can you just tell me your top recommended move and why, in one sentence?

I found that if I play c8 (flipping 6 discs), White can hit back with a1 (flipping 5 back via the b2-c3-d4-e5-f6-g7 diagonal). If I play b7 instead (flipping 5 discs including g7, which kills that a1 threat), White can instead hit back with b6 (flipping up to 6 discs via column b). Both my big moves seem to get punished hard. Is there a move order that avoids giving White either of those huge counters, or is one of these two branches actually still better for me long-term?

parts.content: None

I got greedy chasing flip-counts and didn't see that White's b8 was going to cut through that whole diagonal/column combo I'd just set up with b6. Rough way to learn that in Othello the *last* few moves matter way more than the flashy mid-game captures. Well, lesson noted for next time — thanks for being there even though the assistant wasn't fully cooperating today.

args.question: So I ended up losing 20-44 after playing b6 then g2 near the end. I'm still not clear on why White's b8 reply was so devastating there — was my whole b6 line just losing from the start, or was there an earlier move (like back when I had g2/b6/a7/b7/b8/c8 as options) where I should've played differently to avoid setting up that final collapse?

parts.content: Guess the assistant's still on the fritz — didn't get anything back again. Oh well. My best guess in hindsight is that the whole cluster of empty squares around a3/b6/b7/b8 was just structurally bad for me — every move I made there opened a long diagonal or column for White to exploit later, and I didn't calculate far enough ahead to see the b8 counter coming. Lesson learned for next time: in these tight endgames, the danger squares near corners matter way more than the immediate flip count. That's a wrap on this one.
